canDo: Can combine nominalisation (l’essor, la reconnaissance), modalisation (il semblerait que, à en croire, sans doute) and discourse connectors (d’une part… d’autre part, quant à, certes… mais) to report different positions objectively and put forward a well-supported view of your own.
review: Integrated review of J15–J27: J15 nominalisation, J19 modalisation, J23 discourse connectors, plus J21 sequencing, J24 negation, J26 verb structures and J27 formal register; the theme links to J25 citizenship (language and identity).
input: Read: a long article on the shift in French’s centre of gravity and the debate over the norm, a column against “accent discrimination” and a Belgian’s forum post asking for advice; listen: a sociolinguist on French in African cities, a column on “travelling words” across the French-speaking world and an announcement for a French Language Day writing competition. Strategy: tell “the author’s view” apart from “reported views” and mark modalisation markers.
output: Write: an article for a language school magazine that presents the “single norm vs regional varieties” debate objectively and takes a stance (≥220 words), with at least 3 nominalisations, 3 modalising expressions and paired connectors; speak: a 4-minute monologue on “accent discrimination”, then a debate on “quotas for French songs on the radio”.
checkpoint: Stage check: reading and listening accuracy ≥80%; the reported parts of your essay are clearly separated from your own view; can summarise a long article orally as 5 nominalised headlines within 90 seconds.
challenge: Today’s challenge: find a French-language news item from Africa, Belgium, Switzerland or Quebec on TV5MONDE or RFI, note 1 regional word or expression you don’t know, write a news headline using nominalisation, then write 2 reporting sentences with il semblerait que / à en croire.

questions.why: The article moves from the “shift in centre of gravity” to lexical innovation, education and then the question of the norm (« Faut-il pour autant renoncer à toute norme commune ? »). A is the opposite of « Son essor »; B is the opposite of « signe de sa vitalité ».
« Les académies… fixaient la norme, et l’on considérait volontiers les usages d’ailleurs comme des écarts, voire comme des fautes ». A is the opposite; C has no basis.
« ces mots répondent à des besoins précis : nommer une réalité locale, éviter un anglicisme… ». B contradicts « figurent… au même titre que les mots de l’Hexagone »; C has no basis.

« le français reste avant tout la langue de l’école… Son essor dépendra donc largement de la qualité des systèmes éducatifs ». A contradicts the second paragraph (already in dictionaries); C isn’t stated.
« Il s’agirait moins de choisir entre unité et diversité que d’accepter leur coexistence ». A is rejected by « Rien n’est moins sûr »; B goes against the whole text’s position.
tirer les conséquences de qch = to adjust accordingly to a fact. basculement refers to the fundamental shift in French’s centre of gravity. B and C aren’t what the phrase means.

The author criticises the hierarchy of “authentic French vs copies” and, in the last paragraph, proposes what schools should do. A is just the opening hook; C is rejected by « je ne plaide pas pour que chacun écrive à sa guise ».
« j’ai compris que, pour certains, il existait un français authentique et des copies plus ou moins réussies ». A and B are only the surface tone; the author reads an implicit hierarchy into it.

« les moqueries… peuvent fermer des portes, à l’embauche comme à l’université ». B is rejected by « Il serait naïf d’y voir une simple question de susceptibilité »; C contradicts the several regions listed.
It first concedes that a common language needs rules (concession), then uses Mais to stress that an accent is not a grammar mistake. Neither A nor C matches the function of this structure.
« les enseignants pourraient leur faire découvrir la diversité des usages francophones ». A is exactly what she opposes; B has no basis.
It ends with « Dois-je m’adapter… ? … Vos avis m’intéressent »: after describing his experience, he asks for opinions. B: etymology isn’t covered; C: he says himself « Rien de méchant ».
« Ce qui m’agace, ce n’est pas la remarque en elle-même, c’est l’idée qu’il y aurait une bonne et une mauvaise façon de compter ». A contradicts « Rien de méchant »; C has no basis.
« il figure dans les dictionnaires, et il est d’ailleurs bien plus logique », with quarante and cinquante as the analogy. Neither A nor B has any basis.
renier = to disown, to turn one’s back on; d’où je viens = where I come from. Giving up his home expressions would feel like turning his back on his roots. B and C are literal misreadings.
The interview covers the future of French in Africa, street usage, literature and education. B isn’t covered; C is only mentioned in passing.
« Il ne suffit pas qu’une population augmente… Tout dépendra de la scolarisation ». A is exactly the “shortcut” (raccourci) she warns against; C has no basis.

« Certains y voient un appauvrissement. Moi, j’y vois plutôt une compétence ». A is others’ view, which she reports; B contradicts what follows (these young people can speak standard French at school).
« C’est exactement ce que font les jeunes Parisiens… quand ils changent de registre. Chacun dispose de plusieurs façons de parler ». B and C aren’t her point.
« Ils montrent qu’on peut être un écrivain de langue française à part entière sans imiter Paris ». A is the opposite; C contradicts « lus bien au-delà de l’Afrique ».
« cesser de considérer les langues africaines comme des obstacles… Ce n’est pas une concurrence, c’est une complémentarité ». A distorts it into “replacing”; B is the opposite of what she argues.
The column presents regional words: Belgian drache, Swiss natel, and Quebec’s magasiner / dépanneur. A is only the angle of approach; C isn’t covered.
« vous filez au dépanneur, la petite épicerie du coin ». A is the usual meaning of dépanneur in France, used here as a distractor.
« Il semblerait que les Français empruntent plus volontiers à l’anglais qu’à leurs voisins francophones »; il semblerait que is a cautious modalising expression. B and C aren’t mentioned.
« ouvert à tous à partir de quinze ans ». A and C are wrong restrictions.
« seront lues en public lors d’une soirée festive le 20 mars ». The deadline is 28 February; the rules are already on the website.

V28-01.exZh: The centre of gravity of French is shifting towards Africa.

V28-02.zh: to enter, to be included in
V28-02.exZh: Several Quebec words have been included in the dictionary.

V28-03.exZh: It would seem that the French borrow more readily from English.

V28-04.exZh: This fear of saying the wrong thing has a name: linguistic insecurity.

V28-05.zh: in the medium term, over the coming years
V28-05.exZh: Over the coming years, the town will have to build a new school.

V28-06.exZh: Formal writing needs a reference norm.

V28-07.exZh: Institutions must adjust accordingly to this shift.

V28-08.exZh: Linguistic insecurity keeps some people silent in meetings.

V28-09.exZh: For years, she tried hard to erase her accent.

V28-10.exZh: Associations are calling for full recognition of regional languages.

V28-11.zh: to close doors, to cost someone opportunities
V28-11.exZh: Mockery of an accent can cost people job opportunities.

V28-12.exZh: I’m not arguing that everyone should write as they please.

V28-13.exZh: These words remind us that French belongs to no one.

V28-14.zh: at the same time, in passing
V28-14.exZh: Discovering other usages is, at the same time, learning to respect them.

V28-15.exZh: A colleague corrected me in front of the whole team.

V28-16.exZh: It wasn’t meant unkindly, I grant you, but it was still awkward.

V28-17.zh: for the sake of peace and quiet
V28-17.exZh: Should I change the way I speak for the sake of peace and quiet?

V28-18.exZh: I don’t want to come across as someone who takes offence at trifles.

V28-19.zh: to turn one’s back on one’s roots
V28-19.exZh: Giving up these words feels a bit like turning my back on my roots.

V28-20.exZh: Looking at population alone isn’t enough: don’t oversimplify!

V28-21.zh: a fundamental shift, a turning point
V28-21.exZh: The pandemic brought about a fundamental shift in our working habits.

V28-22.exZh: Teenagers know how to switch register depending on who they’re talking to.

V28-23.exZh: Their novels are read far beyond Africa.

V28-24.exZh: Studies tend to show that the mother tongue helps learning.

V28-25.exZh: By saying magasiner, you’re doing your bit for the French-speaking world.

title: Checkpoint II: reporting and argument
